items.question: Why did you choose RSI over the large AI companies that were trying to recruit you?
items.object: Choosing RSI over large AI companies
items.answer: In the end I chose RSI because, for the current trend in large models, teams are becoming smaller, moving faster, and having less friction within teams. A very small, elite team getting one thing done has become a major trend. Once that trend exists, staying at a big company may no longer be convenient. I have personally witnessed many issues that large teams have. Quite a few large teams wanted to recruit me then: Anthropic, xAI, Amazon, Apple, Microsoft. But you would find that perhaps two or three months after contacting me, many of the people who contacted me had left. Everyone has seen plenty of news, which I will not list one by one. The reason is that large teams and large companies have bloated organizational structures or simply too many people, so problems are inevitable. CEOs are very anxious; they want the company to succeed, so they issue many orders or directives to direct the people below. But large teams need a great deal of time to adapt to those demands from above, while also aligning with employees’ ideas and wishes below. If that is the case, the speed of this process is far slower than the speed at which small teams align. So recently you see many large companies and teams frequently reorganizing, frequently laying people off, and changing direction and strategy. The main reason is that the speed of organizational communication simply can no longer keep up with AI’s pace of development. I had been at Meta for almost 11 years, so I could feel this trend firsthand. During that period, Meta happened to give me this opportunity, so I went to live a different life. That was roughly my thinking.

items.question: Why do you think investors were willing to back your AI company at a $4.65 billion valuation before you had a product?

items.answer: I would put it this way: capital still looks at people. Whether investment, fundraising, the ultimate business vision, or the ultimate product—in AI, a field that changes so rapidly—it is hard to explain everything clearly from the outset. Often you say today that you will do this, and two months later someone else releases something new. Then how does the team respond? Can it execute quickly and produce something? That is the most important thing. What capital values most is judgment about people: their previous experience, their abilities, and how well team members fit and work together. items.question: How do you understand recursive self-improvement as a goal for AI?
items.object: Recursive self-improvement of AI
items.answer: I think it means: can I use AI to optimize many things about AI itself, making AI stronger, and then pull myself upward by stepping on my own left foot and then stepping up again? That is roughly the logic. Specifically, we hope to use AI to do many things people still need to do today—for example, scientists discovering new ideas and new logic, or whether AI can improve the training process, make new discoveries with AI. All of this is within our recursion. Our ultimate vision is a very good system into which I put various computing resources and which outputs new knowledge, new perspectives, and new insights. That is roughly it.

items.question: How do you see AI automating the research and discovery process?

items.answer: At present, when humans or researchers conduct research or make AI discoveries, much of their time is still wasted—perhaps “wasted” is not the right word. Humans have biological limits: you need to eat, drink, use the bathroom, and sleep, so you cannot spend 100 percent of your time on this. I think if AI can at least replace humans in, or do, labor humans consider tedious, burdensome, or repetitive, that is certainly possible. That is the first step. items.question: How do you see the role of human judgment in evaluating increasingly capable AI systems?

items.answer: I think that, at least now, AI still does not meet the human standard of evaluation. So for a certain period, humans can still be evaluators; that is no problem. Second, when AI becomes capable enough, many evaluation standards become subjective rather than wholly objective. For example, AI may follow human instructions very well when writing code. It is not that human capability fails to reach some level; often you complete what you want to do according to each person’s ideas.

items.question: Why do you see interpretability as increasingly important for recursive self-improvement?
items.object: Interpretability in recursive self-improvement
items.answer: I think it is extremely important—indeed, more important than before. One reason is safety. When we launched Recursive, we emphasized that we want to build safe superintelligence. One solution for the safety part is interpretability. If you understand a model’s internal mechanisms and have some ideas about them, you roughly know how it works, and then you know what threats and problems it may pose, especially in the future. That is extremely important. Interpretability also provides a very good indicator for finding what we want faster. For recursive self-improvement, you may need massive compute—thousands or tens of thousands of cards to train a model. If you do not understand the model itself, you may only predict or assess whether it is good after training is complete, which is slow. With interpretability, can we move that evaluation earlier? If so, can we improve computational efficiency? Interpretability plays a very important role in this process.

items.question: How do you see interpretability helping autonomous AI systems make discoveries beyond human capabilities while staying within safe boundaries?
items.object: Interpretability as a way to keep autonomous AI discovery safe
items.answer: I think the main thing is interpretability. If you know what the model has found in the discovery process, humans can evaluate it. That is important. If the model’s own mechanisms can be inspected, we can use that to judge whether it has crossed a boundary or discovered something new without crossing one. You can even use another model to verify whether this model is good. All that is possible. For harder problems, we hope the model finds things humans cannot do, while also keeping it safe. In that situation, we cannot discover new things on the model’s behalf, so we have to know how it thinks, how it reasons, whether it has crazy ideas, and whether in some places it goes beyond what we want it to do. That requires interpretability.

items.question: Why do you find the pursuit of AI that can autonomously conduct research attractive despite its current limitations?
items.object: Developing AI that can autonomously conduct research
items.answer: Precisely because it cannot do it, that is where future researchers can contribute. We of course hope to start a company and enable AI to do it; that is important. This is not a zero-to-one matter—not either impossible or achieved. It is unlike self-driving cars, where either you are 100 percent safe on the road or you hit someone; that will not do. So it has many levels. Maybe AI can write code today but cannot read papers. Tomorrow it can read papers but still cannot understand a problem’s essence. The day after, perhaps it can understand a little, but still cannot understand very hard problems. It rises level by level. There is a very deep staircase. We do not know how far it can be climbed, but we can climb a bit higher. Every step brings many application scenarios and possible directions. That itself is very attractive. Researchers naturally hope to scale scientific heights, so it is a very interesting staircase.

items.answer: I do not think it is wrong. For one thing, it is very practical and everyone uses it, so it definitely is not wrong. items.question: How do you assess the promise of latent-space reasoning as an approach to AI reasoning?
items.object: Latent-space reasoning
items.answer: I think each latent token can store more information than each language token. A latent token can hold a great deal of information—for example, several different lines of thought at once; ultimately one is correct, and then your path emerges. But if you think in language, you must manually write down what every line of thought is, one by one. So the efficiency differs. At least in principle, we can see that difference. Of course, there may be all kinds of differences in implementation and eventual use cases. But the direction itself is interesting. Our Coconut paper has accumulated many citations, and many people have extended it. That includes structures such as the recent Looped Transformer, which itself is latent-space reasoning and has achieved good results. There is probably a lot to explore in this direction, and perhaps it could become an interesting breakthrough point.

items.question: Why do you find grokking—the sudden transition from memorization to generalization in a model—an interesting research problem?

items.answer: I think grokking itself is a very interesting problem: how a model suddenly goes from memorization to generalization. Whether this process can reveal the secret of the entire neural-network training process—that is roughly it. The main logic of the paper is that with some specific, structured data inputs, you can see very clearly the process by which a model goes from memorization to generalization. This process can itself be described by a relatively clear mathematical process. For example, there is an energy function. When data are insufficient, its minimum is always a memorization solution; but after the data become large enough, at a certain point the structure of the energy function suddenly becomes a generalization solution. That is the grokking process. We can also know how much data is needed to produce such a change. So this is very interesting. If we understand it clearly, perhaps we can better understand neural-network training and improve efficiency and speed.

items.question: Why do you agree that the ceiling of pre-training determines the ceiling of reinforcement learning in large language models?

items.answer: Yes, I do agree. We have indeed found that the purpose, and a major utility, of post-training with reinforcement learning is that it takes, say, an answer that originally ranked 200th and moves it into first place. In this way, the model can do some problems better. That is how it works. But the condition is that among the answers to the problem at the outset, at least one must be correct. For example, if you let it try one thousand times or ten thousand times, perhaps most answers are wrong, but maybe one or two are usable. Once that seed exists, reinforcement learning can use that seed to gradually raise it to the top, improving performance in this way. If there is no seed at all, then doing more reinforcement learning is useless. That is why reinforcement learning produces results only after large language models have already become fairly successful. If you only do reinforcement learning, it cannot really generate comparatively deep things. So I think the most important part of large language models is still their pre-training. After pre-training, all kinds of representations emerge inside them. Once they emerge, those representations can, to a certain extent, explain some of the structure in the data. To a certain extent, they can discover, or learn, interesting reasoning patterns in mathematics or in data. These reasoning patterns are gradually amplified through reinforcement learning, ultimately producing an answer. That is how it works. If the earlier reasoning patterns have not been learned particularly well, then later reinforcement learning is useless. So simply betting on reinforcement learning still has a ceiling. That is my view, so I may be wrong.

items.question: How do you see the role of data in making AI models stronger and ultimately achieving human-like efficiency?

items.answer: I think data is still very important. At present, a great deal of user data and human data has already been used. The next question is whether we can create new data. In fact, many of the major advances in this recent wave of models have come from putting reasoning-model data back into earlier pre-training, or into the mid-training process. Through this approach, the model becomes stronger, reaching an initial form of self-evolution. Put another way, you can imagine that once a new model becomes stronger, we could have it generate a great deal of data, then put that data back into pre-training or mid-training. Would that make the model even stronger? That is one possibility. Of course, this process itself is relatively slow and requires a great deal of computing resources. So what comes next? Some people propose continuous learning. Continuous learning means that when new data comes in, we want to learn it deeply without paying such a high cost. That is why people have proposed this concept. But I think the ultimate goal is still this: data may currently be a very important factor for making models strong very quickly, but for a model ultimately to become as strong as humans, or achieve human-like efficiency, we may still need to see whether there are good algorithms or good new paradigms for training the model itself. So that may be the biggest issue. Of course, if we continue along the current paradigm, data is still very important, because if the paradigm does not change, then more data really does produce better results.

items.question: How do you think a newly established NeoLab should approach research when it lacks the resources of a big company?
items.object: NeoLabs’ research challenges and reliance on scaling laws
items.answer: I think ultimately, an important challenge is how to produce research results and make progress quickly in an environment like a NeoLab. That is important. Many NeoLab members previously came from big companies, or places with abundant resources. They could say, “Let’s run an experiment,” and then spend a lot of money to do it. Maybe that experiment cost several hundred million dollars, or even a billion, but the company paid for it. So for a newly established small company like this, a lab like ours, or an entity that needs to raise funding, a very important question is: how can we make this learning process more efficient? We hope to make the whole iteration process and workflow more meaningful, while also discovering new things. That is a major challenge, I think. So whether we will still use traditional scaling laws to do this is something we need to consider. For example, some friends of ours used to work at big companies or other resource-rich places. For them, resources could be unlimited, or at least quite abundant. They could use all kinds of methods to find a good scaling law and make it work. But for us, we may need to think about cost, and think of all kinds of clever ways to avoid simply piling up massive computing resources while achieving better results. That may be a major challenge. If someone has only the mindset of scaling laws, they may not succeed easily. Beyond scaling laws, you still need other new, deeper understandings of the problem in order to succeed. It comes down to research taste.

items.question: How do you see small AI companies’ research directions developing relative to those of large companies such as OpenAI, Google, and Anthropic?
items.object: The relationship between small AI companies’ research directions and those of large AI companies
items.answer: I think they are first and foremost developing in parallel. I have talked with many people at large companies, and I think one issue is that large companies now generally have a tendency toward convergence. The reason is that many directions and plans at large companies are decided by the CEO or senior leadership. Senior leaders may feel they need to chase hot trends: they see this as something they want to do because others are doing it, or because others are doing it well. Because of this top-down structure, large companies become quite homogeneous. Everyone is doing roughly the same thing. For example, once coding agents became hot, everyone made coding agents, because everyone thought, “I want AI to write code.” So even if you want to do something different inside a large company, the environment and pressure push you to work on things related to the company’s main direction. This is a major trend. Ultimately, people in large companies may lack—not the capability; they have the capability—but the time and energy to do things that are inconsistent with the main direction. That becomes very difficult. Naturally, for a small company to produce benefits and results quickly, it will choose directions different from those of large companies. So they are parallel. Only later, for example once a small company’s business is doing well and that direction becomes new, or becomes a new direction everyone is paying attention to, might competition arise. But that is another matter. This has happened many times in history. When Anthropic first worked on code—when it was doing coding—very few people were paying attention. I remember that last year, or perhaps the year before, everyone was grinding math. We pushed AIME very high. But I remember Anthropic saying at every announcement, “We are not grinding this.” When its models were released, there were no math performance numbers. They were grinding coding, and they put up their coding results. In the end, everyone realized this could really make money; it was a very good business model. Suddenly everyone rushed in. So this will probably be a normal pattern in the future. That requires small-company members to have the patience and vision to pursue directions that large companies are not pursuing now.

items.question: Why do you have bosses and employees sit together in your office?
items.object: Shared seating for bosses and employees
items.answer: We do not have anything special, like a place where the boss has to sit and a place where employees have to sit. We all sit together, which makes communication more convenient.
